extracted.intended_audience: editors and editorial staff of biomedical journals (especially in low- and middle-income countries)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards and operational practices for recruiting, training, managing, and incentivizing peer reviewers and for accelerating and ensuring quality in the peer review workflow of biomedical journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of author‑recommended reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask authors to suggest two to three potential reviewers for their studies (practice used by many journals; supported by COPE/DOAJ/OASPA guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are informed that the editor might use one of their suggested reviewers along with reviewers from the journal's database and that comments from suggested reviewers are subject to acceptance. For overseas submissions, suggested reviewers are carefully vetted before being used. This approach can help address reviewer scarcity and increase the reviewer database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of suggested reviewer credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly check credentials of author‑suggested reviewers before using them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check institution affiliation, whether they are faculty, verify and reconfirm their e‑mail, look up their publications and academic accomplishments online. Only once convinced of their academic interest/credentials are they sent a manuscript on a trial basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reviewers with explicit guidelines and structured review forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Send guidelines on how to review a manuscript and how to write a peer review report; share an appropriate Peer Review Performa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer Review Performa for original studies contains about two dozen questions to help reviewers evaluate aspects of the study. Different proformas are used for Reviews, Editorials and Case reports. Providing these helps train reviewers and standardize reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content and quality of reviewer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer reports should be comprehensive and substantive — pointing out what new information the study adds, its significance, and its relevance to clinical practice, along with other methodological and contextual aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or substandard reports are discarded. If a report is inadequate, editors convey observations to the suggested reviewer and to the author who proposed them; the manuscript is reassigned. Comprehensive reviews may prompt the editor to ask for the reviewer's CV and include them in the reviewer database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and retention of reviewers based on demonstrated quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trial reviews and past report quality to decide whether to retain suggested reviewers in the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who produce comprehensive useful reviews are asked for CVs and added to the database and re‑invited; those judged not good enough are not asked again. Trial review performance is used as the main retention criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and privileges to recruit and retain reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer tangible and intangible benefits to reviewers to retain them and encourage quality reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges mentioned include: waiving processing charges for reviewers' own submissions; priority processing of their manuscripts; discounts in publication charges (ranges given); discounts for trainees named by the reviewer; occasional gifts (books); sponsored participation in training workshops or conferences; and consideration of 'token appreciation' for reviewers who don't use other benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts when accepting suggested reviewers (local restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict author‑suggested reviewers who may have conflicts of interest for domestic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For submissions from within the country, authors are advised not to suggest reviewers from their own institution or from the same city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor responsibility for timely processing and final decision authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must ensure speedy processing, give timely feedback, and not unduly delay submissions; editors have the final authority to accept or reject a paper and decide how much weight to give reviewers' comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should avoid sitting on submissions for weeks or months then rejecting them; they must balance authors' impatience with fair, quality review. Reviewers act as advisors, but the editor has final judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑submission structured abstract screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Require a structured abstract with complete author and study details before full submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structured abstract must contain complete details of listed authors, institutional affiliations, and individual authors' contributions. Incomplete abstracts without authors/affiliations are not entertained. Interesting/innovative abstracts are invited to submit full manuscripts with Ethics Committee approval, Letter of Undertaking signed by all authors, and scanned proof of processing fee. Quick initial screening saves authors time and fees by rejecting unsuitable submissions early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional pre‑submission manuscript review service
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer paid pre‑submission review of full papers where editorial resources allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals with larger editorial staff may offer pre‑submission review (for a fee) to help authors revise before formal submission; this prevents wasted time if the paper is unsuitable for the journal. Small journals with limited staff generally cannot offer this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast‑track processing should be limited and equitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast‑track or expedited processing may be offered only in exceptional cases and must avoid creating unfair advantage for those who can pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal discontinued a general fast‑track facility because almost every author requested it and it would have advantaged those with financial resources; editors should be cautious and selective with fast‑track offerings to prevent inequity and resource strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize reviewer and editor training and capacity building
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide regular workshops and formal courses to train peer reviewers and journal editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent workshops on scientific writing and publishing and training of peer reviewers are recommended. Certificate and advanced courses (e.g., Certificate Course in Medical Editing, Diploma in Medical Journalism) help create qualified personnel, improve journals' recognition, and raise overall peer review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider journal policies and infrastructure to increase processing capacity (online only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt policies (like online‑only publication) and seek regulatory flexibility to accommodate more papers and reduce costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If regulatory authorities stop insisting on print copies (for established, indexed journals), journals could publish online only, accommodating more papers and lowering production costs. The editorial notes practical problems with print archives and suggests regulators adopt a rationale approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor preference may be influenced by manuscript citation of the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts that cite articles published in the target journal can positively influence editorial decisions to proceed with processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may give positive consideration to submissions that cite the journal. Nonetheless, acceptance remains at the editor's discretion and subject to peer review.
